reading.body:
The failure here is one of training-data acquisition: Suno and Udio built generative music systems using copyrighted recordings scraped from platforms including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius without obtaining licenses or paying rights holders. Suno acknowledged that its training corpus amounted to essentially all music files on the internet. The deployment failure followed directly from the training failure, because a system trained on unlicensed material then generated outputs close enough to specific copyrighted works that prompts styled after Chuck Berry or Mariah Carey produced near-identical reproductions of their most recognizable recordings.

This is a case where the problem was present before a single user request was made. It was embedded in the choice of what data to collect and how to collect it. Catching it would have required rights clearance decisions at the data-gathering stage, not at the output stage, and the outputs themselves would have needed systematic comparison against known copyrighted recordings before public deployment.

What is not established is that any court outside Germany has issued a final finding of infringement against either company: a German court ruled against Suno in a GEMA case, some parties have settled, and other cases remain in litigation, but a lawsuit is not a verdict, and the allegations of intentional or systematic theft have not been adjudicated to conclusion in most jurisdictions.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music, have sued AI music generators Udio and Suno, claiming they illegally scraped thousands of copyrighted songs to train their systems. The labels allege that both companies copied music en masse without permission or compensation and that their models directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The lawsuits name artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others whose work was allegedly used. The record labels submitted a lengthy list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped.

To support their claims, the labels created AI-generated songs using specific prompts and demonstrated that the outputs closely resemble existing copyrighted recordings. For example, prompts requesting 1950s rock and roll style produced songs nearly identical to Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," and a prompt describing Mariah Carey's characteristics generated a near-perfect copy of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed separately in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, setting up a major legal battle about generative AI services and copyright infringement.
